title: Pride and Prejudice - Chapter III
author: Jane Austen
description: The mysterious Mr. Bingley finally arrives in Hertfordshire, making a grand entrance at the local assembly ball. While Bingley delights the neighborhood with his charm, his friend Mr. Darcy offends the room with his cold pride. This chapter introduces the initial friction between Darcy and Elizabeth following his famous slight of her beauty.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bennet remains intentionally vague about his visit to Mr. Bingley to frustrate his family's curiosity. He enjoys the intellectual power that comes from withholding information in the domestic sphere. This playful antagonism defines his relationship with his wife and daughters throughout the early chapters.

analysis_entries.section_focus: The social currency of Lady Lucas
analysis_entries.paragraph: Lady Lucas serves as the primary conduit for social information when Mr. Bennet fails to provide it. Her favorable report on Mr. Bingley's handsome features and agreeable manners fuels the neighborhood's speculative fire. Information in this society acts as a form of currency that determines social status and marital hope.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: intelligence of their neighbour, Lady Lucas.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Bingley’s return visit to the library lasts only ten minutes and excludes the Bennet sisters entirely. Despite this brevity, the ladies find ways to satisfy their curiosity by observing him from an upper window. The specific details they note—the blue coat and black horse—show how every detail is scrutinized for social significance.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.

analysis_entries.section_focus: The economic attraction of Mr. Darcy
analysis_entries.paragraph: The report of Mr. Darcy having ten thousand a year instantly makes him the most attractive man in the assembly room. This figure is more important to the guests than his noble mien or handsome features. It illustrates the stark reality that wealth often dictates character judgment in the Regency social landscape.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: of his having ten thousand a year.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Public opinion of Mr. Darcy shifts rapidly from admiration to disgust as his proud manners become evident. His refusal to be pleased by local society is seen as an unpardonable insult to the community. This collective judgment establishes the 'pride' and 'prejudice' that will complicate the central romance.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: turned the tide of his popularity;

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Darcy's cold dismissal of Elizabeth as merely 'tolerable' serves as the catalyst for her long-standing prejudice. He explicitly refuses to 'give consequence' to a woman he deems slighted by others. This moment of rejection creates the initial obstacle that defines Elizabeth's early view of his character.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mrs. Bennet's recount of the evening is colored by her desire for her daughters' success and her resentment toward Darcy. She exaggerates Jane's triumph while painting Darcy as a 'horrid' and 'disagreeable' man. Her narrative shows how personal bias can reshape the memory of social events into a moral drama.

anchor.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: related, with much bitterness of spirit, and some exaggeration, the shocking rudeness of Mr. Darcy.
